paragraphs: Wagoner County's biggest data center fight ended without a building. Beale Infrastructure, a San Francisco developer, proposed Project Atlas on 270 acres between Highways 72 and 51B south of Coweta, near the city's wastewater treatment plant. Crowds packed Coweta council and planning commission meetings to oppose it, and in January 2026 the planning commission voted against the development plan. On March 30, 2026 Beale told the city by phone it was withdrawing its rezoning application; the land remains zoned agricultural.

The anger in Coweta was as much about secrecy as about the site. The Frontier found that City Manager Julie Casteen signed a nondisclosure agreement with Beale in May 2024 requiring her to keep secret both the talks and the agreement's existence, and that Mayor Naomi Hogue and Vice-Mayor Jeremy Barnett signed their own by September 2025. Residents called for the city manager to be fired and the mayor and vice mayor to resign. A police criminal inquiry opened in May 2026 found, in June, "no substantiated criminal conduct," while flagging concerns about "public perception, policy discussion, or transparency expectations."

Broken Arrow, which reaches into the county, went the other way before any application arrived. An unnamed company held a letter of intent to buy about 51 acres for a data center that City Manager Michael Spurgeon put at 100 to 150 megawatts. When the letter lapsed, the council on June 15, 2026 adopted a six-month moratorium on data center approvals, with an option to extend six months; the moratorium is listed on the Tulsa County page, where the city's center sits. A staff committee is drafting an ordinance, and Spurgeon has said he may ask for the extension.
The county's map also lists Meta's Project Anthem twice, as east Tulsa and Tulsa entries; the company says the $1 billion campus is in east Tulsa, and it is covered in full on the Tulsa County page.

Amazon Web Services' Project Rainier campus near New Carlisle, which trains Anthropic's AI models, is already running about 910 megawatts of power and is expected to grow to as much as 2,200 megawatts, or 2.2 gigawatts, once the roughly 30-building campus is finished. Construction began in 2024; about 18 buildings were operating as of July 2026, when AWS said it had invested $13.8 billion, past its original $11 billion goal.

Neighbors describe a changed town. Riley Thompson, who lives on family land at the edge of New Carlisle, told TheStatehouseFile.com about workers "flying through" past children and fresh litter on every walk; retired mail carrier Daniel Caruso called the construction-era commute "a nightmare." AWS says the buildings use water for cooling less than 2 percent of the year, but the county's economic development director confirmed actual water use is covered by a nondisclosure agreement. "What is so secret about how much water you use to cool your servers?" Caruso asked.

A second, larger AWS-area proposal collapsed: the county council voted 7-2 in December 2025 against rezoning 1,000 acres of farmland east of New Carlisle for a $12 billion campus, after residents said it would cost them their homes and cited school buses on U.S. 20. The developer may return after six months. Microsoft is separately building a data center near Granger, within Mishawaka.

Republicans on the county council called in August 2026 for a two-year moratorium on new data centers, arguing officials should see how the AWS and Microsoft campuses perform first. Democratic council president Bryan Tanner said "an arbitrary time clock is not a replacement for good judgment" and warned that state lawmakers had nearly stripped local governments of land-use control. No moratorium had been adopted as of the council's late-August debate, and no later vote has been published.

Minneapolis has spent 2026 deciding whether data centers belong in the city. The City Council passed a six-month moratorium on new data centers citywide on June 25, with one exception for smaller downtown projects, and must decide by Nov. 21, 2026 whether to extend the pause or write permanent rules. Minnetrista, which has had no applications, adopted its own one-year moratorium on Aug. 3.

The downtown exception got its first test when Legacy Investing signed to buy the Star Tribune's shuttered printing plant for a 20-megawatt data center. Hundreds of residents opposed it at neighborhood forums in August over its environmental impact and jobs; in September the company withdrew its application and pulled out of the deal. Council member Aurin Chowdhury, the pause's lead author, said the city lacks "a modern regulatory framework for data centers," while Michael Rainville called it "policy by fear, not facts."

Elsewhere the scale is smaller. Robbinsdale approved a variance for a 4,000-square-foot facility that US Internet's chief financial officer called "really a switching station," not one of "the big behemoths." The county's table also lists Digital Realty and T5 Data Centers sites in Minneapolis, with no stage or size yet reported.

Jasper County has two data center proposals, one inside Joplin and one in open country with no zoning at all. In Joplin, local developer Jimmer Pinjuv, who owns the 2,064-acre Wildwood Ranch, sought to annex and rezone land at West 20th Street and Central City Road from single-family residential to heavy industrial so it could be sold to an unnamed developer. The Planning and Zoning Commission approved the preliminary plan 6-1 on January 12, 2026. On January 20 the City Council held a seven-hour meeting, with at least one person removed, and approved annexing 540 acres and rezoning 600. The data company's name was not disclosed. A listing by the Mokan Partnership, a regional economic development group, advertised the site as offering at least 200 megawatts.

"I feel like many residents feel like this was snuck up on, under the wire," resident Jennifer Jones told KOAM before the vote. Amanda Calderon-Kidston of Joplin Citizens Against Wildwood Ranch Data Center Site cited "excessive consumption of utilities, including electricity and gas" and noise. The city says the proposal was brought to it and is not a city project; planning official Troy Bolander said it is requiring 14 feasibility studies, and Pinjuv is working with Liberty Utilities on a study of the load. The Joplin Sustainable Technology Alliance then tried to force a public vote. Its petition to repeal the annexation gathered 2,832 signatures, more than 2,200 short, and a second against the rezoning gathered 2,348, nearly 2,700 short. The council certified both as insufficient, so neither went to an election.

In the east of the county, Bloomington, Minnesota-based Geronimo Power is planning a "hyperscale" data park of several buildings south of Liberty's La Russell Energy Center, near Sarcoxie, with a solar farm of about 2,000 acres and battery storage north of La Russell to partly power it. The company told the Sarcoxie council about it on March 3, 2026, but the site lies outside city limits. Eastern District Commissioner Jimmy Morris said that because Jasper County has no zoning, "there's not a lot the commissioners have a say in," and that the county's role is mainly road and decommissioning agreements. Between 175 and 200 people packed a meeting in Sarcoxie organized by Rhys Hine's group, Say No to Data Centers: Keep Jasper and Lawrence Counties Rural, and the Joplin opponents. "I think it could be the death of La Russell," said resident Linda Heman, whose family cemetery sits across the road from the site. Geronimo's Lindsay Smith says no final decisions have been made.
/data-centers/united-states/missouri/jas.unconfirmed: Dropped: Abits Group as Wildwood Ranch's end user and a 450 MW figure for the Geronimo park (search summaries only); the date the petitions were filed and certified. FourStatesHomepage (KSNF) returned Access Denied to curl. The Sarcoxie meeting story was read on Yahoo News; its originating outlet is not named in the text.

paragraphs: Angelina County's main data center proposal would reuse the old paper mill on State Highway 103 east of Lufkin, a heavy industrial site that employed nearly 600 people before it closed in 2004. County Judge Keith Wright announced the negotiations in his State of the County address in February 2026, naming the developer as Amp Z and calling it a $1.5 billion project, the largest single investment in the county's history.

Wright said it could bring about $4.6 million in county property taxes at full value, 500 construction jobs and 30 permanent ones, and would need tens of megawatts at first and hundreds over time; the company was negotiating power contracts with the Longleaf generating plant and had agreements with Oncor. A Lufkin outlet, the936.com, reported the company's own phasing: about 175 megawatts by 2026, 1.1 gigawatts by 2028 and 2.1 gigawatts once complete. The site covers more than 1,000 acres outside city limits, so Lufkin gets no tax revenue from it.

Residents organized as soon as the news broke, objecting to light, noise, air and water pollution, property values and any tax abatement. In May they were barred from speaking about it at a Lufkin City Council meeting because it was not on the agenda. When dozens came to a Commissioners Court meeting in June, Wright told them the county could not stop it: "We have no authority to do a moratorium or stop any type of development in the county. Texas legislators have consciously limited what counties can do, and they've done it on purpose. They don't trust us." His only leverage, he said, is the tax abatement Denver-based AmpZ Champion Data Center Holdings wants, which he would tie to noise limits, landscape buffers and cleanup bonds. Shelley Tatum, a Democratic candidate for Texas House District 9, urged the court to refuse any abatement, predicting the building would stand empty within ten years.

A second project went ahead with no county vote. HyperDataGrid, a Texas company that builds 20-megawatt liquid-cooled facilities, is developing a data center on the former Northern Chip Mill site on Ben Dunn Road off Highway 103 West; Wright said it had secured power and water agreements and begun clearing land.

On July 14, 2026 commissioners voted unanimously for Resolution 010-26, asking the Legislature to let counties set buffer zones, setbacks, noise and light standards, water impact statements and mandatory public hearings for data centers and battery storage. Lufkin passed a supporting resolution in August. The Legislature does not meet in regular session until January 12, 2027. Commissioners have since hired the law firm Allison, Bass & Magee for help with data center abatement agreements; Wright said the county has signed no nondisclosure agreements.

Bowie County sits on a Southwestern Electric Power Co. transmission line between northwest Texarkana and Valliant, Oklahoma, where at least five data center or solar projects have been proposed in two years. The largest is Project Big Pine, a 500-acre campus at TexAmericas Center announced in April 2026; developer Potentia Development says it could bring $3.5 billion in investment and about 120 permanent jobs. Potentia plans to power the site on site with battery storage in a first phase of 300 megawatts by 2032, growing to 800 megawatts by 2036, while it waits in SWEPCO's grid queue.

The county's own land is also in play. On August 28, 2026, commissioners approved a $12 million sale of 582 acres north of Interstate 30 to Datahub Developers LLC, a company traced to Jackson Healthcare's Georgia offices; no deed, permit or utility agreement had been filed when local reporters checked. Black Mountain Power separately bought 600 acres at Red Lick in March. Texarkana already has a smaller, established data center: a 67,500-square-foot Windstream facility on Olive Street, one of eight the company put up for sale this year.

Residents have packed the commissioners court more than once, with close to 150 attending one meeting this summer. "Don't rubber stamp every project that comes through asking for abatements," Christal Prince told the court. Others cited fire risk from battery storage near the Sulphur River basin and Lake Wright Patman, and the secrecy of nondisclosure agreements. Commissioner Mike Carter said he too opposes a data center but noted the county has no zoning, and pointed to a $100 million lawsuit a developer filed against neighboring Hill County after it passed a moratorium.

Guadalupe County has two large data center campuses under way in its northern end, and both are now the subject of a lawsuit. CloudBurst Texas, an AI campus planned for Francis Harris Lane near the Hays County line, won a tax abatement from the Commissioners Court on a 3-2 vote on April 21, 2026, after the court had rejected an earlier version 3-2 in February. As presented, the campus would have 10 to 12 buildings on about 700 acres and cost an estimated $14.5 billion.

Commissioner Stephen Germann, who voted no both times, said in February, "We are out of water," pointing to farmers' wells going dry; CloudBurst co-founder Cynthia Thompson said the campus would generate its own power with turbines and use 24,000 gallons of water a day. The abatement starts at 90 percent and tapers to full taxes after year 11, and Navarro ISD will tax the full value. Commissioner Jacqueline Ott, an attorney, said the deal gave her "grave concern in both terms of risk and liability."

The county's second project, Palomino Alpha, sits near Zorn beside a major regional power substation. Its reinvestment zone grew in February on a 3-1 vote, with County Judge Kyle Kutscher abstaining because his family owns land in the project area. The Crystal Clear Special Utility District is weighing a request to let the site use up to half a million gallons of water a day; at an August 27 meeting, board member Joseph Benavides said, "It really sounds like they're just telling us what we want to hear."

In July 2026, attorney Bobby Levinski of the Save Our Springs Alliance sued the county and each commissioner on behalf of the Data Center Action Coalition and three residents, alleging Open Meetings Act violations and a conflict of interest over Kutscher's family land sale to Palomino Alpha. The suit asks the court to bar the county from relying on either abatement agreement; the county attorney's office says it does not comment on pending litigation.

The land along FM 2897 southeast of Vernon, around Oklaunion, is where Wilbarger County's data center development is concentrated. Google said in February 2026 that it has a data center under construction in Wilbarger County, to be built alongside new power developed by AES. State licensing filings reported by Data Center Dynamics show two buildings, Project Rise 1A and 2A, each about 991,000 square feet and valued at $500 million, at FM 2897 South. They were filed by Planton Investments LLC and Platon Investments LLC, both giving Google's headquarters as their address, with work starting March 31, 2026 and due to finish by the end of March 2028. Google says the campus will be air-cooled and use water mainly for things like kitchens; it lists the site as "in development" with no opening date.

Water is the local concern. Vernon draws its supply from wells in the Seymour Aquifer, and the Vernon Daily Record describes drought and the data center projects as having made water an increasingly important issue in the county. On September 1 Google announced $4.5 million for Vernon to replace an aging water pipeline, the first grant from a $10 million Texas water program. The Vernon Daily Record noted that the money is separate from the data center and is not an agreement to supply it with water. "Without Google's support, this project would not have been possible," Mayor Pam Gosline said.

A second campus may follow. Through an affiliate, NPDC LLC, Seattle-based Sabey Data Centers now owns 1,245 acres along FM 2897, up from 645 acres a year earlier, and has marketed the site as a campus of up to 200 megawatts. The Record's reporting found test holes drilled for Sabey in August 2024, a 2024 facilities agreement for a "Riley Sabey Interconnection" between Electric Transmission Texas and AEP Texas, and high-voltage current transformers labeled for "AEP 345KV RILEY STATION-SABEY" arriving in Houston in August 2026. Sabey's investment partner still lists the project as pre-development, no customer has been named, and no building construction is on record.

Bitcoin mining got there first. Genesis Digital Assets, a privately held miner with offices in the UAE and the US, runs a mining site at Vernon that it expanded to 70 megawatts in early 2025 with a 10-megawatt container deployment. It takes part in the Texas grid's demand-response program, shutting down during peaks in exchange for payment.
/data-centers/united-states/texas/wilbar.unconfirmed: Dropped: that the site is the retired Oklaunion coal plant (only in GDA's own release as summarised by search); the county's return to extreme drought (seen only as a Vernon Record headline, not read). The Vernon Record's second wastewater permit story refused the connection; KFDX/texomashomepage returned Access Denied. No county commissioners' vote, abatement or moratorium on these projects was found.

paragraphs: The independent city of Manassas covers about 10 square miles, and its data centers sit close to homes. Amazon has built up a string of sites here: in December 2023 the City Council approved selling it about 20 acres of city land on Wakeman Drive, by Manassas Regional Airport, for $27.72 million; it is also building a three-building campus at Dean Drive and Nokesville Road, and in January 2024 paid $152 million for about 140 more acres on Century Park Drive and Vulcan Lane, which fall in Prince William County's data center overlay.

The city has learned that the tax money it expects does not always arrive. Digital Realty's data center on Godwin Drive, which opened in May 2024 on the former Glen-Gery brickyard, turned out to be leased to a bank. Because banks pay Virginia's Bank Franchise Tax instead of most local taxes, the city says it cannot collect business personal property tax on the servers inside, though it still gets about $1.2 million a year in real estate tax; the tenant was not disclosed until a tax return was filed in April 2025. The city may ask the General Assembly to look at the exemption.

Noise has driven new rules. The city treated data centers as warehousing, permitted by right in industrial zones, until a Planning Commission subcommittee reviewed a draft ordinance in August 2025, when Manassas had one completed data center and three sites with seven buildings under development. The draft would require a special use permit in the I-1 and I-2 zones, cap height at 75 feet, and add a 100-foot setback from homes, schools and parks. As of September 2026 the ordinance has not been adopted and no hearing date has been announced. Just outside the city line, residents of the 291-home Great Oak subdivision have complained since 2022 about noise from four nearby Amazon buildings.

Marion County's computing history runs through the I-79 High Technology Park near Fairmont, where the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration runs its Environmental Security Computing Center, used to store climate and weather data and to model forecasts and disasters. NOAA is adding a $100 million supercomputer named Rhea there. West Virginia High Tech Foundation chief Jim Estep called it "one of the first big things that (the park) expansion was in preparation for," and said it would help NOAA use artificial intelligence and machine learning in weather, ocean and climate forecasting.

Next door, a commercial proposal is at the study stage. In May 2026 Hog Lick Aggregates, a limestone and sandstone supplier, said it had begun a feasibility study of a natural-gas-powered microgrid and data center on its 277-acre site in White Hall, cooled geothermally with water from a nearby shuttered coal mine rather than fresh water. The company pitched it as a way to serve the NOAA facility and to fit Gov. Patrick Morrisey's "50 X 50" energy plan. President Brian Redmond acknowledged concerns about "strain to existing infrastructure" but pointed to jobs and tax base. He said there is no timeframe, the study could take several years, and the company is also open to manufacturing or commercial use of the land. The proposal drew criticism on Facebook when it surfaced.

If a project there were certified under the state's 2025 microgrid law, House Bill 2014, local government would have little say. That law bars counties and cities from enforcing ordinances such as noise or pollution limits against certified developments. When the House approved rules to carry it out in February 2026, by 78 to 16, Del. Laura Kimble, a Harrison County Republican, voted no because they still did not restore local control or address water.
/data-centers/united-states/west-virgini.unconfirmed: WBOY returned Access Denied. Dropped: that Hog Lick would need an outside partner to build a data center (search summary only); Rhea's installation date and specifications (NOAA release and Times West Virginia story not read). No county commission vote on a data center in Marion County was found.

paragraphs: HUMAIN is the artificial intelligence company Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund set up in May 2025, during President Donald Trump's visit to the kingdom. It aims to deliver 6.6 gigawatts of data center capacity over a decade. Its chief executive, Tareq Amin, previously ran Rakuten Mobile and Aramco Digital. In its first week it announced a string of chip and cloud partnerships: Nvidia chips drawing 500 megawatts, a separate $10 billion, 500-megawatt effort with AMD covering Saudi Arabia and the United States, a $5 billion "AI Zone" with Amazon Web Services, and inference chips from Groq.

The physical buildout began in August 2025, when HUMAIN broke ground on its first two data centers, in Riyadh and in Dammam in the Eastern Province, each with an initial capacity of 100 megawatts. Amin told Bloomberg then that they would go live in the second quarter of 2026, but that the 18,000 Nvidia GB300 chips already bought still needed US government export approval. In November 2025, at the US-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington, Nvidia and Elon Musk's xAI said xAI would be the first customer of a 500-megawatt HUMAIN facility with about 600,000 Nvidia GPUs; Qualcomm said HUMAIN would deploy 200 megawatts of its chips. In December 2025 Al Moammar Information Systems disclosed a HUMAIN contract to design and build an AI data center worth more than 155 percent of its 2024 revenue, roughly SR1.88 billion. The same month Saudi Telecom Co. agreed a joint venture, 51 percent owned by HUMAIN, to develop AI data centers through its subsidiary center3, starting at 250 megawatts at a site designed for up to 1 gigawatt.

The first confirmed production capacity came on August 31, 2026, when AMD, Cisco and HUMAIN announced that AMD MI355X GPU systems were live in Saudi Arabia and selling compute to customers. The companies said a further 250 megawatts on AMD's MI400 chips would start deploying in 2027, and that their joint venture is on track for up to 1 gigawatt by 2030. These figures are the companies' own. None of the reports read gives the power sources, water use or local permitting of the Riyadh and Dammam sites, or confirms that either 100-megawatt building is fully operating.
/company/humain-pif/.unconfirmed: Dropped: 1.9 GW by 2030 and a $77 billion total (vision2030.ai analysis site, not a news outlet); a Together AI 250 MW partnership (arabfounders.net, not read); claims that the Q2 2026 opening slipped and drone strikes near Dammam (analysis site only). The go-live and 2027-2030 figures come from a company press release and are attributed.

paragraphs: NEXTDC's largest planned site is S7, a large block of land in Eastern Creek on Sydney's western outskirts, bought for A$353 million in October 2024. OpenAI agreed in December 2025 to use some of its capacity. Planning documents filed in March 2026 show nine buildings and a substation, for 612 megawatts of power, more than the 550 megawatts first announced. New South Wales assesses the project directly because of its size, and NEXTDC was still preparing its environmental report in July 2026. Goodman has separately filed for a rival campus of up to 500 megawatts nearby in Eastern Creek.

NEXTDC is Australia's largest independent data center operator, listed on the Australian stock exchange, with about 20 sites running or planned across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide, Canberra and Darwin. Since December 2025 the amount of capacity customers have signed up for has more than doubled, driven largely by a single 250-megawatt deal at its S4 campus in Horsley Park, Western Sydney. By June 30, 2026 customers had signed up for 740 megawatts, though only 175 megawatts was actually running and billing.

To pay for the buildout, NEXTDC raised about A$2.2 billion in April 2026 through a share sale and a debt program backed by the Canadian pension fund La Caisse, then added a further A$2.3 billion of debt in July. Australia is also moving to tighten power rules for data centers: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in July 2026 that large sites will have to put as much renewable power into the grid as they draw, and the national energy regulator has recommended they buy renewable energy certificates and register as market participants.

The fight that defined data centers in Western Australia this year was at Hazelmere, in the City of Swan about 15 kilometers north-east of Perth's CBD. GreenSquareDC, a Sydney-based developer acquired by the Swiss private equity firm Partners Group in March 2025, applied to build a three-storey, AI-ready data center on a 4.5-hectare industrial site on Stirling Crescent, which DCD reported as a 120MW, roughly 15,000 square meter building. The Urban Developer put the project at $600 million. The site sat beside the Helena River Steiner (Waldorf) School and close to the Helena River.

The public comment period drew 1,897 submissions, 1,836 of them objections, citing noise, heat, electromagnetic energy and exhaust. The City of Swan's statutory planning manager, Phillip Russell, conceded the proposal was consistent with the site's zoning but recommended the state's outer metropolitan development assessment panel refuse it for one reason: its 18 diesel back-up generators. "City staff cannot accept that the potential for noise exceedance by the operation of the data centre in an emergency back-up power scenario and its potential nuisance and adverse impact to the amenity of so broad a residential area should be tolerable," he wrote. At a council meeting on May 13, 2026, councillors voted 11-2 for mayor Tania Richardson to speak against the proposal at the panel's May 19, 2026 hearing.

GreenSquareDC withdrew on May 14, 2026, before the hearing. Chief executive Charles Penny said the company still believed the site was appropriate and blamed the requirement to assess its generators at 100 percent load in a full emergency, which he called "an unrealistic and impractical benchmark for the operation of modern-day data centres." Francesca Flynn, executive director of Bibbul Ngarma, which runs a restoration program on the Mandoon Bilya (Helena River), said the site was about 40 meters from the river channel, next to a conservation wetland, on two Aboriginal heritage sites and near a primary school and homes: "This proposal was so inappropriate that it's difficult to identify a less suitable location." The federal member for Hasluck called the withdrawal "a major win off the back of community coming together."

The episode left a planning question open. Swan councillor Sarah Howlett said Western Australia still classifies data centers as "warehouses" for land use, which she said misrepresents their function and the power they need. Elsewhere in the metropolitan area, CDC (Canberra Data Centres) announced in August 2025 a campus at Maddington, 20 kilometers south-east of central Perth, of up to 200MW on completion, with the Australian Financial Review reporting AU$415 million for the first stage, targeted to open in 2026; no opening has been reported yet. CDC says its closed-loop cooling uses no water for primary cooling.

Federal prosecutors and public defenders are trying to stop the TikTok data centre at Pecém from switching on. On September 4, 2026, the federal prosecutors' office (MPF) and the federal public defender (DPU) filed a civil action against Omnia and the state environmental agency Semace; after the court's first order, the state of Ceará and the municipality of Caucaia were added as defendants. Their central argument is that Semace licensed the project through a simplified environmental report (RAS), a route meant for low or medium impact works such as go-kart tracks and rodeo grounds, rather than a full EIA/Rima. The action says the preliminary licence allowed 19,700 litres of water a day and the installation licence 144,000 litres, drawn from groundwater in a region that has declared water emergencies in 16 of the last 21 years and where nearby communities depend mostly on wells. The site is about two kilometres from the Lagamar do Cauípe protected area, which partly overlaps Anacé Indigenous land under study by Funai, and according to the lawsuit Omnia said it did not consider prior consultation of the Anacé an obligation.

Inside the export processing zone (ZPE) of the Pecém Industrial and Port Complex, in Caucaia on the Fortaleza metropolitan coast, Omnia, the data centre arm of the asset manager Pátria Investimentos, is building what Brazilian outlets call the largest data centre in the country, with TikTok owner ByteDance as its client. Works began on January 6, 2026, with vegetation clearance and earthmoving. Canaltech reports two main buildings of 150MW each, the first due in 2027 and the second in 2028; Poder360 reports a first phase of 200MW of IT capacity drawing about 300MW. The total investment is put at R$200 billion over ten years, more than R$100 billion of it for equipment, and the national ZPE council approved five data centres at Pecém in November 2025. Because it sits in a ZPE, all its processing is for export, serving users outside Brazil. It is a different scale from what the state already had: Ascenty's Fortaleza 1 at Maracanaú, 30 kilometres from the submarine cable landings at Praia do Futuro, has 9,000 square metres and 10MW and has operated since 2015. The lawsuit describes the Pecém site as about 70 hectares; Poder360 gives 34 hectares near the CE-348 highway, between Caucaia and São Gonçalo do Amarante.

Power comes under a 20-year, US$2 billion self-production agreement with Casa dos Ventos announced in May 2026, in which Omnia becomes a partner in the wind farms, drawing mainly on the 630MW Ibiapaba wind complex being built in Ceará and partly on the Dom Inocêncio farm in Piauí. The companies say the operation will run on 100 percent new clean energy, a condition of the ZPE tax benefits, and will not compete with local supply or push up tariffs. Canaltech notes the campus will also have 120 diesel generators as backup, and that the five Pecém projects together would reach about 1 gigawatt, which it put at two-thirds of Ceará's generation.

The two institutions want a court order stopping Semace from issuing the operating licence, and the company from energising the site, until the Anacé are consulted and a full impact study is done. Omnia said the project has "solidez técnica e jurídica" (technical and legal soundness), that all its permits were validly issued, and that it had not been formally served. Semace said it had not been notified. TikTok said it would not comment because it is not a party to the case.
/data-centers/brazil/ceara/.unconfirmed: cearaenoticia.com.br is a repost of the Canaltech story and is not used. Launch date conflicts (Mobile Time: presented to Lula September 2025; Canaltech: launched November 2025; Diário do Nordeste: formalized December), so no launch date is given. Jobs figures (4,000 vs 550 operational + 3,800 construction) vary by source and are left out. Ascenty Fortaleza facts come from a DCD Brazil piece that reads as promotional; only size, power and start year are used from it.

paragraphs: Two data centers are being fought in Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. At Alixan in the Drôme, on the Rovaltain site beside the Valence TGV station, the Marseille startup Sesterce had a permit for an AI data center of 40 megawatts of power, expandable to 80, until a judge in Grenoble suspended it on July 10, 2026. Near Lyon, the investor DC Max and Abu Dhabi's Phoenix Group plan an 18-megawatt AI data center at Dardilly, with works due to start in late September 2026 and last 18 months.

At Alixan, a collective called Assez DataCenters, made up of six environmental groups and neighbors, challenged the permit. The judge found the project should have had an environmental impact study and could raise temperatures within 200 meters of the site; work has stopped until a full ruling, which can take years. On July 27 Sesterce said it had appealed to the Conseil d'État, France's highest administrative court.

At Dardilly the permit was signed in January 2025 under the previous council. A petition from the group Nature Dardilly asking for an environmental inquiry has passed 21,000 signatures, in a town of about 9,000. "It uses a lot of energy, it will make noise," said founder Françoise Perraud, whose group wants it moved to an industrial zone. Mayor Patrice Crosnier says it meets environmental rules and has promised a public meeting with the investor this fall; no date has been set.

France 3 reports another data center under construction at Meyzieu, east of Lyon. The grid operator RTE says data centers have reserved about 1.3 gigawatts of grid capacity in the region, about half of all new requests.

Poland's data center growth is centered on Warsaw, and so is the first organized opposition. In Piaseczno, south of the capital, Sien Real, a joint venture of the Polish builder Budimex and Spain's Ferrovial, plans four data center buildings on Energetyczna Street, with a 70-megawatt power connection, under permits issued in 2024; fencing is up and work has begun. Residents protested at the construction fence on September 16, 2026, and Piaseczno's mayor, Daniel Putkiewicz, asked the developer to hold an open meeting for residents on September 29.

Protest organizer Anna Rzewnicka said the nearest house is 35 meters away and each building will be 25 meters tall: "Hałas będzie tu 24 godziny na dobę" (there will be noise here 24 hours a day). The environmental report allows up to 286.48 cubic meters of water a day for all four buildings; the developer says the current design draws up to 55. Residents fear that in a shortage the site would get water first. The mayor has proposed a working group of residents and council members to negotiate water, noise and waste heat with the developer.

A second fight is at Reguły, in Michałowice municipality near Warsaw, where Hillwood plans four large buildings on about 40 hectares, at about 130 megawatts, for an unnamed tenant. About 1,200 people signed a petition against it. Bigger plans are further out: a campus of up to 500 megawatts at Domiechowice near Bełchatów, and WBS Power's Baltic Data Center Campus at Lublewo in Choczewo, which the company says would reach 3.2 gigawatts, a figure not confirmed by the grid operator. Poland's data centers together used about 250 megawatts in 2025.

Qatar's data centers are in and around Doha, where Google began building data centers in 2023 under partnership deals signed with the government in 2020. The country's next step is a $20 billion joint venture between Qai, the AI company of the Qatar Investment Authority, and the Canadian asset manager Brookfield, announced on December 9, 2025. It plans AI infrastructure in Qatar and abroad, including a computing center for the region, but no site or size in Qatar has been announced.

The Qatar Investment Authority says the country's natural gas gives it an edge in powering data centers, and its head of funds, Mohsin Pirzada, told Reuters the fund was investing in data centers before they were in fashion. Qatar's phone company Ooredoo has spun off its data center arm, Syntys, which recently expanded in Doha.

The 2026 war with Iran brought new risk. Iran struck two Amazon data centers in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain in the first days of the conflict, and an outlet linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guard then published a list of 29 "tech targets" in Bahrain, Israel, Qatar and the UAE, including Google, Microsoft and Amazon facilities. Brookfield said in March that the war would not derail the Qatar venture.

Campaigners say Catalonia's government has approved a framework to make the region "the digital port of the Mediterranean," with 26 large data centers planned across the region. Projects above 20 megawatts of power can ask the Generalitat to be treated as strategic, which speeds their permits. The city of Lleida went the other way: in January 2025 its council refused data centers, saying they create too few qualified jobs and use too much energy and water, DCD reported.

The region's flagship so far is MERLIN Edged's 15-megawatt data center for CoreWeave in Barcelona's Zona Franca, opened in May 2025; Equinix also runs its BA1 data center in Barcelona. At Alcover, in the Alt Camp, Scranton Enterprises, the Grifols-linked holding that owns the closed Iberboard Mill paper plant, is lining up more than 20 megawatts of power to turn the site into a data center called Iberdata, and then plans to find a technology partner to build it.

On September 22, 2026, the campaign "No als megacentres de dades a Catalunya" protested at the opening of the AI Summit Barcelona. Led by SETEM, Ecologistes en Acció, the Intersindical Alternativa de Catalunya and the Xarxa d'Economia Solidària, it wants a moratorium on data centers above 5 megawatts until there are rules for transparency and public oversight. "No volem tornar a la política del totxo" (we do not want to return to the politics of the brick), the union said.
